title: From SDLC to ADLC: What Changes When Agents Write the Code
summary: Agents don't erase the SDLC phases. They change who runs each step, how fast feedback comes back and where a person checks the work. Sourced, with a way to start.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Say it's a Tuesday. Before standup you write six lines describing a CSV export: which columns, who can use it, what happens past 100,000 rows. You hand it to a coding agent and head into a meeting. An hour later a branch is waiting for you: the endpoint, a background job, eleven passing tests and a note that says "I wasn't sure whether deleted users belong in the export, so I left them out. Please confirm."

Nobody typed that code. Somebody still has to decide whether it's right, and that somebody is you. That move, from doing every step yourself to setting the goal and judging the result, is what people mean when they talk about going from SDLC to ADLC. This post covers what actually changes, what the numbers do and don't say (checked November 2026), and a sensible way to start.

What moves, and what stays put

Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report, published in January 2026, calls this one of the biggest changes in how we work with computers since the graphical user interface. Big claim. The more useful line in the same report is smaller: the traditional SDLC stages remain, while agent-driven implementation, automated testing and inline documentation shrink the cycle time. Keep in mind that the shrinking part is a prediction for 2026, written by a company that sells a coding agent.

So you still plan, design, build, test, ship and maintain. What changes is who does each step, how many steps run at once and how fast feedback comes back. The unit of work goes from "a person doing a task" to "a person directing agents that do tasks, then checking what comes back."

A quick note on the name. ADLC isn't a standard with a spec behind it. Some people expand it as Agentic Development Life Cycle and mean software built mostly by agents, which is how this post uses it. Others, like IBM, use "agent development lifecycle" for the process of building and running AI agents themselves. If someone at work drops the acronym, ask which one they mean.

The classic SDLC loop

The lifecycle most of us learned runs through eight phases. People do each one, and each one is mostly signed off before the next starts.

It's predictable, which is why it lasted so long. It's also slow to learn. QA arrives after the code is written, so problems show up late. Scope gets fixed early, so a change halfway through ripples back into design and estimates. And the lessons wait for a retro at the end, when it's too late to use them on this project.

The agentic loop

The agentic version keeps the loop and changes the cast. Agents take most of the execution steps, often several at once, and one step stays with a person on purpose.

Going clockwise: you define the goal (intent, outcomes, limits), turn it into a PRD or spec an agent can work from, and write the skills it needs, meaning the instructions, tools and project conventions it should follow. Then you split the work and hand it out. Agents write and refactor code, then run tests and evals against it. Next comes the human step: you read the results, check traces and dashboards, correct course and approve. Only then does the change deploy, and monitoring feeds what happens in production back into the next goal.

The split-and-hand-out part has real tooling today. In Claude Code, for example, each subagent runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, tool access and permissions (Claude Code docs, checked November 2026). That's what lets a research agent, a test-writing agent and an implementation agent work side by side without tripping over each other's context.

Six shifts, side by side

Here's the comparison in one table. Read the right column as "where teams are heading", since few teams run all six today.

DimensionClassic SDLCAgentic loop
Who does the workPeople run every phase by hand.Agents run most execution steps. People direct and approve.
PlanningScope, budget and requirements get fixed up front.The team revises goals and the spec as agent output shows where the hard parts are.
SpeedA phase waits until the previous one is signed off.Several subagents work on separate pieces at the same time.
TestingQA is its own phase after implementation.Agents run tests while they code, on every change.
Change mid-cycleA new requirement means replanning and rework.You update the spec and the agents redo the affected pieces.
FeedbackLessons wait for the retro at the end.Production monitoring feeds straight into the next goal.

What the numbers say, and what they don't

The headline examples are impressive. In Anthropic's report, Rakuten engineers asked Claude Code to implement an activation vector extraction method in vLLM, an open-source library of about 12.5 million lines in several languages. The agent finished in a single seven-hour autonomous run, and its result matched the reference method with 99.9% numerical accuracy. The same report says CRED, a fintech platform with over 15 million users in India, doubled its execution speed after rolling Claude Code across its development lifecycle, and credits the gain to developers moving to higher-value work while staying involved.

Now the other side. In a randomized trial in early 2025, METR had 16 experienced open-source developers work through 246 real issues in large repos they knew well. With AI tools allowed, they took 19% longer. Before starting they expected a 24% speedup, and afterwards they still believed they'd been about 20% faster. METR now marks that result as out of date. Its February 2026 update says developers are probably sped up more in early 2026 than a year earlier, and also calls its new data only very weak evidence for how big that gain is.

Google's 2025 DORA report, built on nearly 5,000 survey responses, adds the team view. About 90% of respondents use AI at work, AI adoption is now linked to higher delivery throughput, and 30% trust AI output only a little or not at all. DORA sums it up by calling AI an amplifier of an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses.

How to read all this

Vendor case studies show what's possible on tasks picked to suit agents. Controlled studies show how hard productivity is to measure, and how easy it is to feel faster than you are. Anthropic's own research, cited in the same report, found developers use AI in roughly 60% of their work but can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of tasks. Plan around that range, and measure your own team before and after.

What changes in your day

If your first thought is "so am I being replaced?", the evidence so far points elsewhere. The repetitive execution moves to agents: boilerplate, wiring, first-pass tests, routine refactors. What grows is the work around it. You write goals sharp enough to act on, design the system, set up the skills and tools agents use, and tell a good result from one that's confidently wrong. One engineer quoted in Anthropic's report put it well: they mostly use AI "in cases where I know what the answer should be or should look like", a sense they built by doing software engineering the hard way.

The biggest habit change is review. When an agent can produce a few thousand lines in an afternoon, reading every line with the same care stops working. You still read code. You pick where to read closely: auth, money, data migrations, anything you can't undo. Everywhere else you review outcomes. Does it meet the goal? Do the tests cover the nasty inputs? Does the diff touch things it shouldn't? You type fewer lines and own more of the result.

Five steps to start without drama

Trying all of this at once is a reliable way to lose a sprint. Here's a path where each step builds on the last:

  1. Start with one agent on tests. Tests are small and checkable: if the agent writes a bad one, you see it fail or you spot it in two minutes of reading. It's a cheap place to learn how the agent works.
  2. Write specs and skills as if a teammate will read them. Agents do what you wrote, gaps included. List the goal, the limits, the files that matter and what "done" looks like. There's more on this in prompting is mostly clear communication.
  3. Split one big task three ways. Pick a feature with clean seams (API, UI, migration) and give each piece its own subagent and its own context. Running in parallel is where most of the speed comes from, and the seams also show you where your architecture is tangled.
  4. Move most of your review to outcomes. Agree up front which code paths still get line-by-line reading. For the rest, review the tests, the interfaces and the edge cases.
  5. Wire monitoring back into the loop. Error rates, latency and drift alerts tell you what an agent's change did in production. Feed them into the next goal so the loop learns from every release.

Why one step stays human

The checkpoint holds the loop together

Agents can be confidently wrong. They also work fast and in parallel, so one bad assumption can spread to several branches before lunch. Keep a person approving anything irreversible: production deploys, data deletion, permission changes, payments. Keep observability on so you can see what the agent actually did. That's why the agentic loop puts manual evaluation right before deployment.

There are two easy ways to get this wrong. One is writing it all off as hype and watching other teams ship faster. The other is trusting agents too much and shipping fast, fluent mistakes. The good spot is in between: try it early, write goals precisely and check results like your name is on the release, because it is. For deciding how much freedom an agent should get, see how to give AI agents more autonomy step by step.

Try this week

  • Pick one repo and let an agent write tests for a module you know well. Read every test it writes.
  • Rewrite your next ticket as a spec an agent could follow: goal, limits, relevant files, definition of done.
  • Agree with your team which code paths always get line-by-line review.
  • Measure one number before and after, such as cycle time for small PRs, so you're not guessing.
  • Name the human checkpoint before deploy, and the person who owns it.

The phases of building software are all still there. The typing moved to agents and the judgment stayed with you. If agents are new to you, AI agents, explained without the hype is an easier place to start.

faqs.q: What is ADLC, and how is it different from SDLC?
faqs.a: ADLC usually stands for Agentic Development Life Cycle. It keeps the plan, build, test and ship loop of the classic SDLC, but AI agents do most of the execution steps, often in parallel. People set the goal, write the spec and skills the agents follow, and approve results at a human checkpoint before deployment. The phases stay. Who runs them, and how fast feedback comes back, is what changes.

No. It's a label that spread through 2025 and 2026, and it has more than one meaning. Some people use it for software built mostly by agents. IBM and others use "agent development lifecycle" for the process of building and running AI agents themselves. When someone uses the term, ask which meaning they have in mind.

faqs.q: Will AI agents replace software engineers?
faqs.a: The evidence so far points to the work changing more than disappearing. Anthropic's 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report cites internal research where developers use AI in roughly 60% of their work but can fully delegate only 0 to 20% of tasks. Repetitive execution moves to agents, while goal setting, system design, review and judgment take a bigger share of an engineer's day.

faqs.q: How should a team start with agentic development?
faqs.a: Start small, with one agent writing tests for a module you know well. Then write clearer specs, split one feature into parallel pieces for subagents, agree which code paths still get line-by-line review, and feed production monitoring into the next goal. Keep a person approving anything irreversible before deploy.

faqs.q: Are the productivity gains from coding agents real?
faqs.a: Some are, and they vary a lot. Anthropic reports a seven-hour autonomous run at Rakuten and doubled execution speed at CRED. METR's randomized trial found experienced developers 19% slower with early-2025 tools, and its February 2026 update says gains are likely larger now but still hard to measure. Measure your own team before and after.
